opus-5.5.text:
I think of auto-formalization as the foundation everything else sits on. If you want an AI system to generate conjectures that are actually meaningful, you need a reliable way to check them. Otherwise you end up with a flood of plausible-sounding statements and no way to tell which are true, which are trivial, and which are just subtly ill-posed.

Lean gives you that ground truth. Once a statement is formalized correctly, the proof checker doesn't care how confident the model sounds. It either compiles or it doesn't. But that only helps if the translation from natural language into Lean is faithful. If the formal statement quietly drops a hypothesis or changes a quantifier, you've proven something, just not the thing you meant. So getting auto-formalization right is really about building a trustworthy bridge between how mathematicians think and write and what a machine can verify.

There's also a data reason. Almost all of human mathematics lives in natural language, in papers, textbooks, and lecture notes. Only a tiny fraction has been formalized. If you can auto-formalize well, you unlock that whole corpus as verified training data and as a library of known results. A conjecture-generating system needs to know what's already been established. Otherwise it keeps rediscovering known theorems or proposing things that contradict existing results.

And then there's the feedback loop. Conjecture generation is ultimately a search problem. You propose, you try to prove or disprove, and you learn from what happens. That loop only works if the verification step is cheap, automatic, and correct, and auto-formalization is what makes it automatic. If you skip it, a human expert has to check every candidate, and that doesn't scale.

So it's less that conjecture generation is less exciting. Honestly, it's probably the most exciting part. But if you build it on shaky formalization, you can't trust anything it produces. We'd rather build the verification layer carefully first, so that when the system says it has found something interesting, we actually believe it.

fable-5.1.text:
Because formalization is the foundation everything else rests on. If you want a system that generates new conjectures, you need a way to know whether those conjectures are even well-posed, let alone true. Lean gives you that: a statement that compiles and a proof that checks is not a matter of opinion, it's a fact. But the bottleneck has always been getting mathematics from the way humans actually write it, in papers and lecture notes and informal arguments, into that formal language. Today that translation is slow and expensive, and it's done by a very small number of people.

So if the auto-formalization step is weak, you've broken the chain right at the start. Imagine a model proposing a thousand candidate conjectures. If the translation into Lean is wrong even ten percent of the time, you have no idea whether a proof you find is of the statement you intended, or of some subtly different one. You'd be proving things nobody asked about. The whole point of using a verifier is to remove that ambiguity, and sloppy formalization quietly puts it back.

There's also a data argument. The reason we can't just train a model to be a great mathematician the way we train it to be a great coder is that the formal corpus is tiny. Mathlib is wonderful, but it's a fraction of mathematics. Most of the real knowledge is locked in natural language. If we can formalize reliably at scale, we unlock that corpus, and then every downstream capability, proving, searching, and eventually conjecturing, has something to stand on.

And honestly, conjecture generation is the part people find exciting, but it's also the part where it's easiest to fool yourself. A model can produce something that sounds deep and is either trivial, already known, or false. Having a tight formal loop is what keeps us honest. So we're deliberately doing the less glamorous thing first. Get the translation right, get the verification tight, and then when the system starts proposing new mathematics, we'll actually be able to trust what it says.

astra-6.text:
I think of auto-formalization as building the foundation for conjecture generation. If you start with a conjecture in natural language, you first need to make precise what it says—what the assumptions are, what the objects are, and what exactly you’re claiming. Translating that into Lean gives you a statement you can then try to prove and have the proof checked.

But there are two distinct questions: did you formalize the intended statement, and did you prove that formal statement? Lean helps with the second; getting natural-language-to-Lean right is crucial for the first. Otherwise, you could produce a perfectly valid proof of something you didn’t mean.

Conjecture generation adds another layer: is the statement interesting or useful? I’d want a reliable way to express and check the mathematics before asking a system to propose new mathematics. Auto-formalization doesn’t solve that whole problem, but it gives us a much firmer foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think auto-formalization gives you a foundation for conjecture generation. Before asking a model to propose new mathematics, you want to know that it can faithfully translate what a mathematician means into a precise statement that Lean can check. Otherwise, you might generate something that sounds interesting, but formalize a different claim—or prove something trivial because the assumptions were wrong.

Once that translation works reliably, you can close the loop: formulate a conjecture, try to prove it, and use that feedback to refine it. Auto-formalization doesn’t tell you whether a conjecture is interesting, but it helps ensure that the thing you’re exploring is actually the thing you intended.
